opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that instruction following and innovation are fundamentally different kinds of problems.

When we train a model to follow instructions, the target is relatively clear. A human tells you what they want, and there's a reasonably well-defined notion of whether you did it well. You can collect preference data, train a reward model, and do RL against it. The signal is dense and the goal is given to you. The model is essentially learning to be a very capable executor.

Innovation is different because the goal itself isn't given. You have to decide what's worth doing. A researcher doesn't just solve a problem someone handed them; they notice that something is interesting, that there's a gap, that a certain direction might pay off even though nobody has verified it yet. That requires a kind of judgment about value under huge uncertainty, and we don't have a good way to supervise that.

Part of it is the reward problem. In RL, everything comes down to what you reward. For math or code, you can check whether the answer is correct, which is why reasoning models have improved so much there. But how do you reward a genuinely new idea? By definition it isn't in your data, and its value may only become clear months or years later. The feedback loop is extremely long and sparse, and humans themselves often disagree about what's innovative.

There's also an exploration problem. Today's models are trained largely on human data, so they're very good at producing what is likely given what's already known. Innovation often means going to places with low prior probability, trying things that look wrong at first, and persisting through many failures. Pretraining pulls a model toward the center of the distribution, while innovation lives at the edges. Getting a model to explore meaningfully, not just randomly, is still an open challenge.

And finally there's long-horizon autonomy. Real innovation isn't a single brilliant answer. It's a long process: forming hypotheses, running experiments, interpreting messy results, revising your direction. That requires an agent that can work coherently over a long time, manage its own goals, and learn from its environment. We're making progress on agents, but we're still early in getting them to sustain that kind of open-ended, self-directed work.

So to me, moving from instruction following to innovation means moving from "do what I say well" to "figure out what's worth doing, and then do it." That second part touches the hardest problems in RL: reward design, exploration, and long-horizon learning. That's why I think it's difficult, and also why I find it one of the most exciting directions to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says innovation’s value is difficult to supervise and reward, but does not state that innovation can only be guided directionally.

r002.rationale: It contrasts checking whether an instruction was done well with judging whether a new idea is worthwhile, which may be uncertain and only become clear much later.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't really know what innovation is, in a form we can write down as a training objective.

Instruction following is tractable because the signal is clear. You give the model a task, it produces an answer, a human or a verifier says whether that answer matched what was wanted. Everything in the current paradigm, pretraining, SFT, RLHF, even the reasoning models, is built on that loop. The model gets better at producing things that someone already knows how to evaluate.

Innovation breaks that loop in a fundamental way. If I ask a model to find a new result, by definition nobody has the answer key. The reward signal is sparse, it's delayed, and often it's wrong, because the person judging it may not recognize a genuinely new idea when they see it. Look at the history of science, a lot of important work was rejected at first. So the question becomes, what are you optimizing against? If you optimize against human preference, you get things humans already like, which is almost the opposite of novelty.

The second difficulty is exploration. In reinforcement learning, the hard problems were always the ones with sparse rewards, where you have to try many things that look useless before something clicks. Language models are trained to be very good at producing the high-probability continuation. That's the whole point of the objective. But innovation lives in the low-probability tail. You're asking a system whose entire training pushed it toward the expected answer to now deliberately go somewhere unexpected, and to do that in a directed way, not just randomly. Those two pressures conflict.

Third, innovation usually requires a very long horizon. A real research project is months of trying things, failing, updating your beliefs, and coming back. Current agents can do maybe hours of coherent work. Beyond that, errors compound and the model loses track of what it has learned. Humans handle this with a persistent, evolving world model and with taste, this sense of which direction is promising before you have evidence. We don't have a good way to train taste.

And the last point, which I think people underestimate, is that most innovation comes from interacting with the world, not from reading about it. You run the experiment, the result surprises you, and the surprise is the information. Models that only consume text are seeing the output of other people's surprises. To really innovate, the system needs to be in the loop with reality, and that's expensive, slow, and hard to scale compared to just adding more data.

So it's not that I think it's impossible. I think the recipe that got us here, scale plus imitation plus verifiable reward, is specifically shaped for the problems where answers exist. Getting past that probably needs new ideas about reward, about exploration, and about memory. Those are research problems, not engineering problems yet.

r001.rationale: The response says innovation requires going somewhere unexpected “in a directed way, not just randomly,” communicating that it needs directional guidance.

r002.rationale: It contrasts checking whether an answer matched an instruction with evaluating innovation, which lacks an answer key and may not be recognized as valuable or new.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that following instructions and innovating require different kinds of judgment. When you give an AI a clear task, you’ve already done an important part of the work: you’ve decided what problem matters and what a good answer should look like. The AI can then work toward that target.

With innovation, the target itself may be unclear. You have to ask a useful question, challenge an assumption, or pursue a direction that initially looks unpromising. And producing something different is relatively easy; producing something different that actually matters is much harder.

That also makes training and evaluation difficult. If we reward an AI mainly for answers people already recognize as good, we may encourage conventional answers. But if we reward novelty alone, we can get nonsense. The challenge is helping a system explore uncertain ideas, test them against reality, and develop judgment about which ones are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response says innovation may have an unclear target and requires exploration, but does not state that innovation can only be guided directionally.

r002.rationale: It contrasts working toward a predefined task and answer with judging whether an innovation is useful and matters, distinguishing completion from evaluating innovation quality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think instruction following and innovation require different kinds of judgment. When you follow an instruction, someone has already defined the problem and, usually, what a good answer should look like. With innovation, you have to ask whether you’re even working on the right problem. You need to identify what’s missing, propose something uncertain, and figure out how to test it.

That also makes learning harder. We can often evaluate whether a model followed an instruction. But if it proposes a new idea, how do we know whether that idea is useful, or simply sounds novel? The feedback may require an experiment, and the result may take a long time to arrive.

So I don’t think the challenge is just making models more creative. They can already generate many possibilities. The harder part is developing the judgment to choose a promising direction, pursue it through failures, and produce evidence that something actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says innovation involves choosing a promising direction, but does not state that innovation can only be guided directionally.

r002.rationale: It contrasts evaluating whether a model followed an instruction with judging whether a new idea is useful or merely novel.
